concepts.name: CRR: Definition, Legal Basis and Maintenance Mechanism
key_dimensions: Statutory basis under Section 42(1) of RBI Act, 1934 — NOT Banking Regulation Act
Maintained as cash balances with RBI — no physical cash held in bank vaults counts
Calculated as a percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)
UPSC trap: CRR earns NO interest for banks — opportunity cost dimension

concepts.name: SLR: Definition, Legal Basis and Eligible Assets
key_dimensions: Statutory basis under Section 24 of Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — NOT RBI Act
Maintained in form of gold, cash, or approved securities (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs)
Key distinction: SLR assets are held by the bank itself, unlike CRR held with RBI
UPSC trap: SLR can earn returns (interest on G-secs) unlike CRR

concepts.name: Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL): Composition and Calculation
key_dimensions: Demand liabilities: savings accounts, current accounts, demand drafts — payable on demand
Time liabilities: fixed deposits, recurring deposits — payable after fixed period
Net concept: inter-bank liabilities are netted out to avoid double counting
Both CRR and SLR are expressed as percentage of NDTL — common base for both

concepts.name: Statutory Limits and Floor/Ceiling for CRR and SLR
key_dimensions: CRR: No statutory floor or ceiling after amendment — RBI has discretionary power to fix any rate
SLR: Statutory minimum floor of 0% and maximum ceiling of 40% under BR Act
Historical context: CRR was previously capped at 3% floor and 20% ceiling — removed by Finance Act 2006
UPSC trap: SLR still has a statutory maximum (40%) but CRR has NO prescribed limits now

concepts.name: CRR vs SLR: Functional Differences and Monetary Policy Roles
key_dimensions: CRR directly drains liquidity from the banking system; SLR channels credit toward government
CRR is a pure monetary tool; SLR serves dual purpose — liquidity + fiscal financing
Increasing CRR/SLR is contractionary; decreasing is expansionary
SLR reduction enables more credit for private sector (crowding-in vs crowding-out)

concepts.name: Entities Covered Under CRR and SLR Obligations
key_dimensions: CRR applies to Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) — listed in Second Schedule of RBI Act
SLR applies to all commercial banks including non-scheduled banks, cooperative banks, and RRBs
UPSC trap: NBFCs are NOT required to maintain CRR or SLR — a frequent exam trap
Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks also subject to CRR and SLR requirements

concepts.name: CRR Maintenance: Fortnightly Average and Daily Minimum Requirements
key_dimensions: Banks must maintain CRR on a daily basis with a fortnightly average requirement
Daily minimum: 90% of the required CRR balance must be maintained each day
Shortfall in CRR maintenance attracts penal interest from RBI
Penal rate: Bank Rate + 3% for first day; Bank Rate + 5% for subsequent days of default

concepts.name: SLR and its Relationship with Government Securities Market
key_dimensions: SLR creates captive demand for government securities — supports fiscal deficit financing
State Development Loans (SDLs) are eligible SLR securities — important for state finances
Held-to-Maturity (HTM) portfolio of banks is directly linked to SLR securities
RBI's Statutory Liquidity Ratio gradually reduced from 38.5% (1991) to 18% (current) — financial liberalization

concepts.name: Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) and its Interaction with CRR/SLR
key_dimensions: Banks parking excess funds under LAF (reverse repo) and borrowing (repo) — distinct from CRR/SLR
SLR securities are used as collateral in repo operations under LAF
UPSC trap: LAF corridor (repo–reverse repo) operates above and below policy repo rate
Banks can borrow against SLR securities but cannot pledge CRR balances

concepts.name: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) and SLR Borrowing Window
key_dimensions: MSF allows banks to borrow overnight funds from RBI by dipping below SLR by up to 2% of NDTL
MSF rate is higher than repo rate — acts as ceiling of LAF corridor
Key distinction: MSF allows temporary SLR breach; CRR cannot be breached similarly
UPSC trap: MSF was introduced in 2011 monetary policy — relatively recent instrument

concepts.name: CRR as a Tool for Managing Excess Liquidity vs Interest Rate Transmission
key_dimensions: CRR hike is a blunt instrument to mop up excess liquidity — used during inflationary periods
Unlike OMOs or LAF, CRR does not involve RBI paying interest — zero-cost sterilization
CRR changes affect money multiplier directly — credit creation capacity of banks
Recent use: RBI raised CRR in May 2022 as emergency measure before rate hike cycle

concepts.name: Money Multiplier and Credit Creation: Impact of CRR Changes
key_dimensions: Money multiplier = 1/CRR (simplified) — inverse relationship
Higher CRR → lower multiplier → less credit creation → monetary contraction
UPSC trap: Money multiplier is theoretical maximum; actual multiplier is lower due to cash leakage
SLR also reduces lendable resources but effect on multiplier is less direct than CRR

concepts.name: Incremental CRR (I-CRR): Temporary Sterilization Tool
key_dimensions: I-CRR introduced by RBI in August 2023 to absorb excess liquidity post Rs. 2000 note withdrawal
Applied on incremental NDTL above a specified base date — targeted sterilization
I-CRR is a temporary measure, not a permanent statutory requirement
Distinction from regular CRR: applies only to incremental deposits, not entire NDTL

concepts.name: SLR Securities: HTM Category and Mark-to-Market Exemption
key_dimensions: Banks can classify SLR securities under HTM — exempted from mark-to-market losses
HTM limit linked to SLR percentage — provides accounting relief to banks during rate hike cycle
UPSC relevance: Rising interest rates reduce bond prices — HTM exemption protects bank balance sheets
RBI periodically revises HTM ceiling — important for banking sector stability analysis

concepts.name: Distinction Between CRR/SLR and Other Regulatory Reserves (Capital Adequacy vs Liquidity)
key_dimensions: CRR and SLR are liquidity ratios — ensure banks can meet short-term obligations
Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR/CRAR) is a solvency ratio — distinct from CRR/SLR
LCR (Liquidity Coverage Ratio) under Basel III overlaps with SLR purpose — UPSC overlap trap
NSFR (Net Stable Funding Ratio) — another Basel III metric distinct from SLR but functionally similar

concepts.name: Impact of CRR and SLR on Bank Profitability and Credit Availability
key_dimensions: High CRR/SLR reduces lendable resources — raises cost of funds for banks
Banks compensate by charging higher lending rates — affects credit affordability
Financial repression argument: mandatory SLR forces banks to lend to government at below-market rates
Narasimham Committee (1991) recommended gradual reduction of CRR and SLR for financial liberalization

concepts.name: Cooperative Banks and Regional Rural Banks: Special CRR/SLR Provisions
key_dimensions: State Cooperative Banks and District Central Cooperative Banks maintain SLR under BR Act provisions
RRBs maintain SLR at rates prescribed by NABARD/RBI — may differ from SCB rates
UPSC trap: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are NOT required to maintain CRR or SLR
Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are covered under SLR but have historically different regulatory treatment

concepts.name: Historical Trajectory of CRR and SLR: Financial Liberalization Context
key_dimensions: Pre-1991: CRR was as high as 15% and SLR at 38.5% — peak financial repression era
Narasimham Committee I (1991) recommended CRR reduction to 3-5% and SLR to 25%
Current levels: CRR at 4% (as of 2024) and SLR at 18% — significant reduction over three decades
Reduction in CRR/SLR freed up resources for private credit — financial deepening indicator

concepts.name: Payment Banks and Small Finance Banks: CRR/SLR Applicability and Special Features
key_dimensions: Payment Banks must invest minimum 75% of demand deposits in SLR-eligible G-secs/T-bills
This 75% requirement is ABOVE the standard SLR — special prudential requirement
Small Finance Banks subject to standard CRR and SLR like SCBs
UPSC trap: Payment Banks' 75% investment norm is separate from the SLR mandate — serves similar but distinct purpose

concepts.name: CRR/SLR and Transmission of Monetary Policy: Effectiveness and Limitations
key_dimensions: CRR/SLR changes have slower transmission compared to repo rate changes — blunt instruments
Effective monetary transmission requires low SLR — banks otherwise park funds in G-secs instead of lending
Excess SLR holding by banks (above mandatory) signals weak credit demand — economic slowdown indicator
RBI's preference shifted toward LAF and OMOs over CRR changes for liquidity management post-2000
